title: Soya Chunks Nutrition: The Real Protein Numbers, Dry vs Cooked
meta_description: Dry soya chunks pack about 52g protein per 100g — among the highest of any Indian pantry staple — dropping to roughly 16g per 100g once hydrated and cooked. Full macro breakdown, amino acid profile, cost per gram protein, and how to stop them tasting spongy.
meta_keywords: soya chunks protein nutrition, soya chunks protein per 100g, meal maker nutrition facts, nutri nuggets protein, soya chunks cost per gram protein, soya chunks amino acids
quick_answer: Dry soya chunks (nutri-nuggets/meal maker) contain approximately 52g protein per 100g — one of the highest protein densities of any food in an Indian kitchen. Once soaked and cooked, that same 100g absorbs water and roughly triples in weight, bringing the cooked protein content down to about 16g per 100g. A realistic serving of 50g dry (about 150g cooked) delivers approximately 24–26g protein at only 200–220 kcal, and at typical retail prices that works out to under ₹0.40 per gram of protein — cheaper than almost any other protein source in the pantry.

faq.question: Are soya chunks a complete protein?
faq.answer: Yes. Soy protein contains all nine essential amino acids in meaningful amounts, which is unusual for a plant source — most legumes and grains are missing or low in at least one. Soya chunks are also notably rich in lysine, the amino acid that wheat and rice are typically low in, which makes them a useful complement to a roti- or rice-heavy meal.

faq.question: Do soya chunks lose protein when you hydrate and cook them?
faq.answer: No protein is lost — what changes is the weight. Dry soya chunks absorb water during soaking and cooking and roughly triple in weight, so the same amount of protein is now spread across three times as much mass. That is why dry chunks show approximately 52g protein per 100g while cooked chunks show approximately 16g per 100g — it is a dilution effect, not an actual protein loss.

faq.question: Is it safe to eat soya chunks daily? Do they affect hormones?
faq.answer: For most healthy adults, yes. The concern about soy and estrogen comes from isoflavones, plant compounds that weakly interact with estrogen receptors, but large human studies have not found that normal dietary soy intake meaningfully disrupts hormones in men or women. A daily serving of 40–60g dry soya chunks, used as one of several protein sources rather than the only one, is a reasonable and well-tolerated amount.

intro: Soya chunks — sold in India as nutri-nuggets or meal maker — get recommended constantly as a cheap vegetarian protein, but the protein number people quote depends entirely on whether anyone specified dry or cooked weight. The two figures are very different, and neither is wrong, which is exactly why the confusion persists. Here is the full picture: what actually happens to the protein when you hydrate and cook them, how the amino acid profile stacks up, what they cost per gram of protein, and how to stop them coming out spongy and bland.

sections.heading: The numbers: dry vs hydrated, per 100g
sections.body:
Dry soya chunks are extremely protein-dense because almost all their weight is defatted soy flour that has been extruded and dried:

• Dry soya chunks (100g): approximately 52g protein, 345 kcal, 33g carbohydrate, 13g fibre, 0.5g fat

Once soaked in hot water (10–15 minutes) or boiled directly, soya chunks absorb several times their dry weight in water. Cooked and drained, 100g of dry chunks yields roughly 250–280g of hydrated, cooked chunks:

• Hydrated/cooked soya chunks (100g): approximately 16–17g protein, 100–110 kcal, 10g carbohydrate, 4g fibre

Both numbers are correct — they are just describing different weights of the same food. The protein hasn't gone anywhere; it is simply diluted across the water the chunks have absorbed. This is the same reason cooked rice has less "protein per 100g" than the dry grain it came from.

sections.heading: Why soya chunks are unusually complete for a plant protein
sections.body:
Most plant proteins are missing or low in at least one essential amino acid — dals tend to run low in methionine, for instance, which is why pairing dal with rice (rice supplies methionine, dal supplies lysine) has been standard Indian practice for centuries.

Soy protein is one of the few plant sources that contains all nine essential amino acids in reasonable amounts, including lysine — the amino acid most Indian staples (wheat, rice, most dals) run short on. This is why soya chunks pair particularly well in a roti- or rice-based meal: they fill a gap the rest of the plate tends to leave open, rather than duplicating what dal already provides.

sections.heading: Cost per gram of protein: soya chunks vs the rest of the pantry
sections.body:
Dry soya chunks retail at approximately ₹150–200 per kg in most Indian cities. At 52g protein per 100g, that works out to roughly ₹0.30–0.40 per gram of protein — among the cheapest protein sources available anywhere in an Indian kitchen.

For comparison, using figures from typical Indian retail prices:

• Soya chunks (dry): ₹0.30–0.40 per gram of protein
• Masoor dal (cooked): ₹1.0–1.2 per gram of protein
• Eggs: ₹1.2–1.4 per gram of protein
• Chicken breast: ₹0.9–1.1 per gram of protein
• Paneer: ₹1.9–2.2 per gram of protein

Soya chunks are not close competition on price — they cost roughly a third of what dal costs per gram of protein, and less than a fifth of paneer. The tradeoff, as anyone who has cooked them badly knows, is texture and flavour rather than nutrition or cost.

sections.heading: Why they taste spongy — and how to actually fix it
sections.body:
The spongy, rubbery texture people associate with soya chunks almost always comes down to two mistakes: under-seasoning and not squeezing out the soaking water before cooking.

What actually works:

1. Soak in hot (not boiling) water for 10–15 minutes, then squeeze each handful firmly to remove as much water as possible before adding to the pan. Waterlogged chunks stay bland no matter how long you cook them, because the water inside dilutes whatever masala you add.
2. Marinate the squeezed chunks in a little ginger-garlic paste, chilli powder, and salt for 15–20 minutes before cooking — soya is very absorbent and takes on flavour quickly once the excess water is out of the way.
3. Cook them in an actual onion-tomato masala base rather than boiling them in plain water with spices added after — the chunks need to simmer in fat and masala to develop flavour, the same way paneer does in a curry.
4. Use them in familiar formats rather than trying to make them a standalone dish: soya keema (minced and cooked like keema), soya chunk curry, soya biryani, or soya pulao all work well because the format already expects a chewy, absorbent protein.

Done this way, soya chunks are closer to a blank canvas than a bad ingredient — the sponginess is a preparation issue, not an inherent property of the food.

sections.heading: How much soya chunks to hit a protein target
sections.body:
A practical daily serving is 40–60g dry soya chunks, cooked into a curry or keema-style dish, which yields:

• 40g dry (about 120g cooked): approximately 21g protein, 140 kcal
• 50g dry (about 150g cooked): approximately 26g protein, 175 kcal
• 60g dry (about 180g cooked): approximately 31g protein, 210 kcal

As with any single protein source, soya chunks work best as one of three or four sources across the day rather than the only one — pair a soya chunk sabzi at lunch with dal, curd, or eggs elsewhere in the day rather than relying on soya chunks alone to hit a full protein target.

key_takeaways: Dry soya chunks contain approximately 52g protein per 100g; cooked and hydrated, that becomes approximately 16–17g per 100g — the protein isn't lost, it's diluted by absorbed water
Soy protein is one of the few complete plant proteins, and its lysine content complements roti- and rice-based Indian meals that tend to run low in it
At roughly ₹0.30–0.40 per gram of protein, soya chunks are among the cheapest protein sources in an Indian kitchen — well below dal, eggs, chicken, or paneer
The spongy texture problem is almost always under-seasoning and not squeezing out soak water, not a flaw in the food itself
A 50g dry serving (about 150g cooked) delivers roughly 26g protein at under 200 kcal, best used alongside dal, curd, or eggs rather than as the only protein source in a day
